articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro @ $1,199 packs in more AI
articles.summary: Apple has introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, bringing major upgrades across performance, on-device AI, cameras, battery life and thermal management. At the heart of the new Pro models is the A20 Pro chip, which delivers significant gains in CPU, GPU and neural processing while enabling more powerful on-device Apple Intelligence features. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 in the US.The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max also introduce a new 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture, giving users greater control over light, depth of field and the overall look of photos and videos. Apple has also added new professional camera controls, improved video capabilities and enhanced AI-powered photography tools.iPhone 18 Pro launched at $ 1,119 The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are powered by the new A20 Pro chip, built around a redesigned architecture focused on performance and efficiency. The chip features a six-core CPU with new performance and efficiency cores, with CPU performance up to 20% faster than the previous generation. The GPU has also received a major upgrade, with a seven-core design delivering significant gains in graphics performance and AI-powered image generation.The new neural engine is specifically designed for on-device AI workloads, with a 32-core design and support for advanced 8-bit floating-point operations. Together, the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine improvements make the A20 Pro significantly more capable of running demanding Apple Intelligence features directly on the iPhone. Apple has also increased memory bandwidth by 50%, helping the device handle larger AI models and demanding applications more efficiently.More powerful Apple Intelligence and SiriThe new Pro models bring deeper Apple Intelligence capabilities, including access to Apple's latest Foundation models and more powerful on-device AI models. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro can run its most advanced on-device models yet, enabling features such as enhanced image generation, smarter photo editing and more capable Siri interactions.Siri is also getting a major upgrade. Users can interact with Siri more naturally, continue conversations across Apple devices and use the assistant to take actions across supported apps. Siri can understand information displayed through the camera and help users act on what they see. Apple Intelligence also brings more personalised capabilities, including creating automations through natural-language instructions, finding information across apps and generating images through Image Playground.Apple says the new capabilities will work across more than 3,000 apps, allowing developers to integrate Apple's AI features into everyday workflows.New 48MP camera with variable apertureOne of the biggest upgrades comes to the camera system. The iPhone 18 Pro introduces a new 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture, giving users more control over how much light enters the camera and how much of the scene remains in focus.The variable-aperture system can automatically adjust depending on the scene, while also allowing users to manually control the aperture for greater creative flexibility. A wider aperture can create a shallower depth of field, while a narrower aperture can keep more of the scene in focus. Apple has also introduced new Pro controls, allowing users to manually adjust settings such as white balance, exposure, histogram and shutter speed.For video creators, the iPhone 18 Pro adds more advanced controls and improved cinematic capabilities. Users can adjust shutter speed for motion blur, while AI-powered smart focus tracking can maintain focus on moving subjects. The new system also supports improved Dolby Vision HDR video and enhanced audio recording capabilities.New tools for photographersApple is also expanding its computational photography capabilities. Photographic Styles now offer additional control over texture and grain, allowing users to create more distinctive looks while retaining control over colour and skin tones. The iPhone 18 Pro also introduces a new approach to preserving image authenticity. Apple says captured images can retain additional information that can be used to verify what was actually recorded by the camera.Together with the new variable-aperture camera and Pro controls, Apple says the system is designed to offer greater flexibility for both everyday photography and professional workflows.Improved thermal managementApple has redesigned the thermal architecture of the iPhone 18 Pro to help sustain the higher performance of the A20 Pro chip. The new thermal system features a next-generation vapour chamber with three times the surface area of the system used in the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple has also introduced new thermal materials, including a nano-twin copper material designed to move heat away from the display more effectively. The company says the redesigned thermal system can deliver up to a 40% improvement in sustained performance compared with the previous-generation Pro model.Longest battery life ever on an iPhoneBattery life is another major focus of the new Pro models. The iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max delivers up to 45 hours, giving the Max model the longest battery life ever offered on an iPhone. Apple has also improved charging, with the iPhone 18 Pro capable of reaching 50% charge in around 15 minutes under supported conditions.More connectivity and iOS 27 featuresThe iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also benefit from new software and connectivity features in iOS 27. Apple says AirDrop transfers are up to 80% faster, while connectivity has been improved with smarter transitions between Wi-Fi networks. A new feature called iPhone Handoff allows a single phone number to be used across two iPhones, with the number becoming active on whichever iPhone the user picks up. The Pro models also feature an upgraded Dynamic Island, while iOS 27 brings further customisation and improvements across apps including Mail and other system experiences.iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max price and availabilityThe iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 in the US. Pre-orders for both models begin September 12, with availability starting September 18. With the A20 Pro chip, deeper on-device Apple Intelligence, a new variable-aperture 48MP camera, improved thermal architecture and the longest battery life ever on an iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max represent Apple's biggest Pro upgrade across performance, photography and AI.

articles.title: Microsoft is funding a bet on mud
articles.summary: Warblers and sparrows call across the treetops at sunrise. Deer browse the shrubs. Black bears turn over roots for insects. Above ground, this stretch of North Carolina's Inner Banks looks like farmland, cotton and soybeans and corn running to the horizon.The reason scientists and investors have converged on this 60-square-kilometre tract is underneath it: dense, spongy peat, up to five metres deep, the Associated Press reported.Decades ago, an abandoned farming venture cut 80 kilometres of ditches through the site and drained the water out of soil that had taken thousands of years to accumulate. That left it exposed to drought and fire, altered the habitat, and turned a carbon store into a carbon source. The site now emits about 130,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year."Our goal is for perpetuity to conserve these lands so they can't become oil and gas fields, so they're not mined for phosphorus or turned into parking lots and shopping centers," Tripp Wall, chief executive of the Colorado-based company Pantheon Regeneration, told AP. He described peatlands as underappreciated systems that had been climatologically resilient for 10,000 to 15,000 years "until we screwed them up."Why peat matters more than forestPeatlands cover roughly 3% of the planet's land surface. They hold close to a third of all soil carbon, which is about twice as much as the biomass of every forest on Earth combined, according to the UN Environment Programme.The mechanism is simple. When peat is waterlogged, decomposing plant matter sits in an oxygen-starved environment and the gases stay trapped, while the vegetation on the surface keeps pulling carbon dioxide out of the air. Drain it and the process reverses.That reversal is now a significant emissions source in its own right. UNEP's Global Peatlands Assessment put emissions from drained and degraded peatlands at around 4% of annual human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, from an area equal to roughly 0.4% of the world's land surface. The AP report cites a higher current figure of about 6% of the annual global total.Two-thirds of temperate peatlands, mostly in Europe and the United States, have been dewatered. About 45% of tropical peatlands have been similarly disturbed. Boreal peatlands in Canada and Russia remain roughly 90% intact but face thawing permafrost, intensifying fires and pressure from mining and critical minerals exploration.Only 17% of the world's peatlands sit inside a protected area, according to a study published in Conservation Letters, the journal of the Society for Conservation Biology, in February 2025. For comparison, protected areas cover 38% of tropical forests, 42% of mangroves and 50% of saltmarshes."This is the black gold"Neal Flanagan pushes a metal tube down through roots and buried logs until it sinks about a metre, then pulls out a core packed with black soil. Near the top it is dry, full of dead fibres from wood fern and blueberry. The middle is crumbly and odourless, flecked with charcoal from old fires. The saturated bottom is half carbon and has the consistency of axle grease."This is the black gold," said Duke University ecologist Curtis Richardson, letting ancient peat ooze from his fist. Its "magnitude and importance cannot be underestimated," he told AP.The North Carolina variety, called Pocosin peat, formed from coastal pine forests and evergreen shrubs decaying over millennia. Domed peatlands of this type exist only along the Eastern Seaboard. In North Carolina alone, 17,700 kilometres of canals drain peatlands into coastal estuaries, Richardson said.Fires that burn underground for monthsSaturated peat is close to fireproof. Only surface vegetation and a few inches of peat burn, releasing nutrients and regenerating seed banks.Dry peat is a different proposition. Fire moves underground and can smoulder for weeks or months, drying out and consuming even the saturated layers below.A 2008 fire that started during a drought burned above ground for three months and smouldered underground for four more, damaging over a quarter of the neighbouring Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge and dropping the ground level by several feet in places, refuge manager Sarah Toner said. Where water-level restoration had already begun, the fire burned less deeply.A more recent fire burned about 800 hectares nearby four years ago, lowering the ground by half a metre in places. The North Carolina Forest Service and other agencies put it out in roughly three weeks by pumping water from nearby lakes."We'll lose 5, 6 feet of peat in a matter of weeks, which equates to millions of tons of carbon loss, ancient carbon loss that we simply can't ever get back in human lifetimes," Richardson said.That risk is why Pantheon is prioritising drained sites over intact ones. "There's this urgency to start with what's degraded now," Wall said, "before it goes away."The business modelThe restoration itself is not novel. Pantheon plans to block the ditches to raise the water table, then remove invasive species and replant native grasses and flowers, an approach modelled on projects run by nonprofits and government agencies, including at the adjacent 453-square-kilometre Pocosin Lakes refuge, one of the largest peatland restorations in the United States. That refuge supports red wolves, yellow pitcher plants and Atlantic white cedar, and has become a stopover for migrating tundra swans.What is different is how Pantheon intends to pay for it. The company plans to sell carbon credits to technology companies and other corporations offsetting their own emissions, then use the proceeds to restore and permanently conserve about 4,047 square kilometres of peatland from Virginia to northern Florida over the next decade. Microsoft is among the investors providing initial capital for land acquisition, Wall said. Each credit represents one tonne.Carbon credits carry a reputational problem. Over the years, some programmes have been found to overstate how much carbon they captured, and others were outright fraudulent.Pantheon says its credits will be scientifically verified, drawing on Richardson's decades of data on carbon loss at the site, continuous groundwater monitoring, a tower measuring gas absorbed and released, computer modelling and core sampling, with results checked by an outside third party.What comes backSteve Apfelbaum, a plant and animal ecologist running breeding and migratory bird surveys at the site, stops his SUV on a rutted lane to listen. He picks out prairie warblers, a species in decline."We heard hundreds of them today," he said. "What that tells me is that this ecosystem is really important" for their migration. He also hears Nashville warblers, which call from treetops but nest in cavities in the peat.Native reptiles, plants, fish and insects should follow, said Vladimir Roosevelt, Pantheon's operations director. The company released a pair of red wolves two years ago that have since had pups.All of it, Apfelbaum said, depends on getting the water back into the ground first, a solution he argued gets less attention than tree planting."We've all been bear-hugged and distracted by trees," he said, "when it's really soil and peat that hold the most carbon."(With inputs from AP)

Americares lands its biggest gift ever
articles.summary: A Connecticut family that will not be identified has given $50 million to the American aid group Americares, the largest single donation in the organisation's 47-year history, the Associated Press reported on Wednesday.The gift lands at an unusual moment. Most global health organisations have spent the past year and a half contracting. Americares is now planning to expand."They definitely understood the moment and wanted to do more to respond to that," Christine Squires, the president and chief executive of Americares, told AP of the donor. The family has been associated with the organisation for three decades and is, in her words, very savvy about global health.Also read: MacKenzie Scott's $100 million donation helped wipe out $40 billion in medical debt—here’s how Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife's strategy worksHalf the money will go toward the group's target of helping 100 million people access quality healthcare by 2030, largely by supplying medicines and equipment to its network of more than 4,000 health centres. The focus will be on under-funded countries in sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, North Africa, Asia and Latin America. Americares also plans to increase support for health centres inside the United States, in states where it expects a rise in the number of residents without insurance. The other half goes into the endowment.What was lostAmericares drew roughly 10% of its funding from the US government before the cuts, Squires told AP. The shortfall showed up as cancelled work.A maternal care project in Tanzania lost its support last year. Medical clinics in Colombia serving Venezuelan migrants stayed open for several months on private money before closing. A planned five-year collaboration to build a more resilient medical supply chain across Gaza was scrapped entirely.The organisation now funds itself entirely through individual donors, corporations and private foundations, which Squires said matters as it responds to more than 20 active emergencies, among them the Nepal floods and the Ebola outbreak in Congo.Founded in 1979 and headquartered in Stamford, Connecticut, Americares says it has delivered more than $17 billion in humanitarian aid across 164 countries.The bigger holeThe gift is the latest in a series of private interventions since the Trump administration dismantled the US Agency for International Development in early 2025. The scale of what was withdrawn makes the arithmetic difficult. US foreign aid totalled about $64 billion in 2023, the most recent year with comprehensive figures.Private money has moved, though unevenly. British hedge fund manager Chris Hohn stepped in to keep production running at MANA Nutrition, one of two American manufacturers of the therapeutic peanut paste used to treat severe child malnutrition, after US stop-work orders halted their lines. Hohn had already given the organisation more than $250 million before the crisis.A group of former USAID staff, working outside office hours or after being fired, assembled a list of 80 high-impact programmes and took it to private donors. Their effort, Project Resource Optimization, mobilised more than $110 million in grants, with other emergency funds raising at least $15 million more, taking the total past $125 million within eight months.In March 2025, Jacklyn and Miguel Bezos, the parents of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, committed up to $500 million to UNICEF's Child Nutrition Fund, structured as a one-to-one match designed to draw in other donors. It was, by UNICEF's own account, the largest investment the agency had ever received from a family. The Gates Foundation, separately, narrowed its priorities.Susan Appe, an associate professor of public administration and policy at the University at Albany who researches how nonprofits handle shifting donor-country priorities, told AP that global health has drawn most of the large donors' attention, which she called reasonable given that lives are at stake. But she said the philanthropic response overall has been slower than researchers in her field expected."I think that a lot of philanthropy scholars like myself have been a bit disappointed with the lag of response," she told AP. "It's kind of, to some degree, business as usual."Nobody involved argues that private giving can substitute for what was cut. A study published in The Lancet in June 2025, analysing data from 133 countries, estimated that USAID-supported programmes had prevented more than 91 million deaths between 2001 and 2021, and projected that sustained cuts could result in over 14 million additional deaths by 2030, including more than 4.5 million children under five. The authors described the projection as a model output with a wide uncertainty range.Also read: Bill Gates never studied at University of Washington, but it paid him $500 as a teen; 5 decades later, Microsoft co-founder is giving it $540 millionThe Trump administration has defended the closure. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in July 2025 that the agency had little to show for itself since the end of the Cold War, and that the State Department would prioritise trade and investment over aid, negotiating directly with countries rather than through nonprofits and contractors.Squires said she hopes the anonymous gift prompts others. A donation of that size signals that people still trust both her organisation and the humanitarian sector, she told AP."It's not only up to individuals," she said. "However, individuals who have the means, who have the passion and can invest like this, will help to bring others along."(With inputs from AP)

Homebuyers' body FPCE on Wednesday said real estate regulatory authorities in states have failed to properly implement realty law RERA and pointed out that an estimated 27.6 lakh homebuyers are stuck with delayed projects across the country.

DGCA restricts flying activities at UP training schools during Brics summit
articles.summary:
Flying Training Organisations (FTOs) operating from Uttar Pradesh will not be permitted to undertake flying activities for three days during the BRICS Summit in Delhi as part of enhanced security measures, according to the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA).
In a communication to all FTOs, the DGCA said the restrictions would be in force from 7 am on September 11 to 11 pm on September 13 in view of the BRICS Summit-2026 being held in the national capital.
The order specifically states that "no aircraft including light/micro-light aircraft, hang gliders, helicopters etc. is permitted to fly even to start from any FTO" located in Uttar Pradesh during the specified period.
The restriction will also apply to FTOs located in Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh, according to the communication dated September 7.
